questions.stem: A time series plot displays:
options: the five-number summary of a variable, plotted as a box and whiskers
values of a variable recorded at regular intervals, plotted against time
two numerical variables measured on each individual, plotted together
the frequency of each category of a variable, plotted as vertical bars
questions.explanation: A time series plot shows how one variable changes over time, with time on the horizontal axis and the points joined in order. A scatterplot shows two numerical variables measured on the same individuals.

questions.stem: In a time series plot, time is placed on:
options: the horizontal axis
the vertical axis
both axes
neither axis
questions.explanation: Time is the explanatory variable in a time series, so it goes on the horizontal axis. The variable being tracked, such as sales or rainfall, goes on the vertical axis.

questions.stem: In a time series, the trend is:
options: the difference between the largest and smallest values in the series
the long-term direction of the data, such as increasing or decreasing
a regular pattern that repeats at the same time each calendar year
an unsystematic, short-term fluctuation caused by a one-off event
questions.explanation: Trend is the long-term increase or decrease in the series. A regular, calendar-related pattern is seasonality, and one-off short-term changes are irregular fluctuations.

questions.stem: Seasonality in a time series refers to:
options: systematic, calendar-related movements that repeat over a fixed period
the long-term upward or downward direction of the whole time series
unsystematic, short-term movements that cannot be predicted in advance
the gradual smoothing of a series by averaging neighbouring values
questions.explanation: Seasonality is a pattern tied to the calendar, such as higher electricity use every winter, that repeats each cycle. The long-term direction is the trend.

questions.stem: Irregular fluctuations in a time series are:
options: movements that happen only at the start and end of a calendar year
unsystematic, short-term movements, such as a spike after a one-off event
regular movements that repeat at the same time every calendar year
long-term movements that show the overall direction of the series
questions.explanation: Irregular fluctuations are random or one-off movements that do not follow a pattern, such as a sales spike during a cyclone warning. Repeating calendar movements are seasonality.

questions.stem: Monthly visitor numbers to a Gold Coast theme park are higher every January, April, July and December, and the overall level rises slowly over 5 years. The plot shows:
options: an increasing trend with no seasonality
irregular fluctuations with no trend
an increasing trend with seasonality
a decreasing trend with seasonality
questions.explanation: Peaks in the same months every year are seasonality, here linked to school holidays, and the slowly rising level is an increasing trend. The repeating peaks rule out irregular fluctuations alone.

questions.stem: Weekly sales at a hardware store show no long-term rise or fall and no repeating pattern, apart from one very large week when a storm damaged many homes. The best description is:
options: seasonality only, with a peak in the same week each year
a decreasing trend with one irregular fluctuation
no trend or seasonality, with one irregular fluctuation
an increasing trend with strong seasonality each year
questions.explanation: With no long-term movement there is no trend, and with no repeating pattern there is no seasonality. The storm week is a one-off, unsystematic movement, which is an irregular fluctuation.

questions.stem: Daily customer numbers at a café are high every Saturday and Sunday and low every Monday. Over several months this pattern is best described as:
options: an increasing long-term trend
irregular fluctuations only
a decreasing long-term trend
seasonality with a weekly cycle
questions.explanation: Seasonality is any systematic pattern that repeats with the calendar, and it can have a weekly cycle as well as a yearly one. Because the pattern repeats every week, it is not irregular.

questions.stem: The main purpose of smoothing a time series with a moving average is to:
options: increase the number of data values available for forecasting
make the largest value in the series equal to the smallest
reduce fluctuations so that the underlying trend is easier to see
remove the trend so that only the seasonal pattern remains
questions.explanation: A moving average replaces each value with the mean or median of a group of neighbouring values, which evens out irregular and seasonal movements and reveals the trend. Smoothing leaves fewer values, not more.

questions.stem: A simple moving average is usually calculated over an odd number of points so that:
options: each smoothed value is always larger than the data it replaces
the seasonal indices always add to the number of seasons
the number of smoothed values equals the number of data values
each smoothed value sits at the middle time period of its group
questions.explanation: With an odd number of points, such as 3, 5 or 7, the group has a middle time period, and the smoothed value is placed there. An even number of points has no middle period, so the result would need an extra centring step.

questions.stem: A time series has values 12, 15, 18, 14, 20, 22, 19. The 3-point moving mean centred on the fourth value (14) is:
questions.explanation: The group is the third, fourth and fifth values: (18 + 14 + 20) ÷ 3 = 52 ÷ 3 ≈ 17.33. Centring on the third value instead gives (15 + 18 + 14) ÷ 3 ≈ 15.67.

questions.stem: A time series has values 12, 15, 18, 14, 20, 22, 19. The 5-point moving mean centred on the third value (18) is:
questions.explanation: The first five values are averaged: (12 + 15 + 18 + 14 + 20) ÷ 5 = 79 ÷ 5 = 15.8, placed at the third time period. 17.8 is the next 5-point mean, centred on the fourth value.

questions.stem: A time series has values 12, 15, 18, 14, 20, 22, 19. The 3-point moving median centred on the fourth value (14) is:
questions.explanation: The three values are 18, 14 and 20; in order they are 14, 18, 20, so the median is 18. 17.33 is the 3-point moving mean of the same group, not the median.

questions.stem: A time series has values 12, 15, 18, 14, 20, 22, 19. The 5-point moving median centred on the fifth value (20) is:
questions.explanation: The five values centred on the fifth are 18, 14, 20, 22, 19; in order 14, 18, 19, 20, 22, so the median is 19. The 5-point moving mean of the same group is 18.6, and 18 is the moving median centred one place earlier.

questions.stem: A 5-point moving mean is applied to a time series of 20 values. The number of smoothed values obtained is:
questions.explanation: Two values are lost at each end, because the first and last smoothed values are centred on the third and eighteenth data values. That leaves 20 − 4 = 16 smoothed values.

questions.stem: Daily ticket sales at a cinema show a strong weekly pattern. To smooth out this pattern with a moving mean, the number of points used should be:
questions.explanation: A moving average that spans one full cycle averages out the seasonal pattern, and one week of daily data is 7 points, an odd number. A 3- or 5-point mean would still be affected by the weekly peaks.

questions.stem: Compared with a moving mean, a moving median is often preferred for smoothing a time series that:
options: has a perfectly linear increasing trend over time
has an even number of data values in the series
contains a few extreme values from one-off events
contains values that are all very close together
questions.explanation: The median is resistant to outliers, so a single extreme value from a one-off event does not drag the smoothed values up or down. A moving mean includes every value and is affected by outliers.

questions.stem: Daily visitors to a gallery for one week were 310, 295, 302, 288, 340, 410, 395. The 7-point moving mean, and the day it is placed at, are:
options: about 334.3, placed at the fourth day
about 334.3, placed at the seventh day
about 310.0, placed at the fourth day
about 340.0, placed at the fifth day
questions.explanation: The sum is 2340, and 2340 ÷ 7 ≈ 334.3. With 7 points the middle is the fourth day, so the smoothed value is placed there. 310 is the median of the seven values, not the mean.

questions.stem: A seasonal index of 1.15 for the March quarter means that sales in that quarter are typically:
options: 115% above the average quarter
15% above the average quarter
15% below the average quarter
1.15% above the average quarter
questions.explanation: A seasonal index compares a season with the average season, where 1 (or 100%) is average. An index of 1.15 is 115% of average, which is 15% above it.

questions.stem: For quarterly data, the seasonal indices should add to:
questions.explanation: Seasonal indices average 1, so four quarterly indices add to 4, or 400% as percentages. Monthly indices would add to 12.

questions.stem: Three of the quarterly seasonal indices for a business are 0.9, 1.2 and 1.1. The fourth seasonal index is:
questions.explanation: Quarterly seasonal indices add to 4, so the fourth is 4 − (0.9 + 1.2 + 1.1) = 4 − 3.2 = 0.8. Assuming they add to 1 is impossible here, since the three given already exceed 1.

questions.stem: Eleven monthly seasonal indices for a surf shop add to 11.04. The seasonal index for the remaining month is:
questions.explanation: Monthly seasonal indices add to 12, so the missing index is 12 − 11.04 = 0.96. 1.04 comes from reversing the subtraction around 1 rather than 12.

questions.stem: When using the average percentage method, the first step for each year of quarterly data is to:
options: subtract the mean of that year's values from each of the four quarterly values
divide each value by the value for the same quarter in the previous year
find the mean of that year's values and express each value as a percentage of it
find the mean of each quarter across all years and divide it by the overall mean
questions.explanation: In the average percentage method each value is expressed as a percentage of its own year's mean. Those percentages are then averaged across the years for each season to give the seasonal index.

questions.stem: In one year a shop's quarterly sales were 40, 60, 80 and 20 (thousand dollars). Using the average percentage method, the Q2 value as a percentage of the yearly mean is:
questions.explanation: The yearly mean is (40 + 60 + 80 + 20) ÷ 4 = 50, and 60 ÷ 50 × 100 = 120%. Dividing by the yearly total of 200 gives 30%, which is a share of the year rather than a comparison with the mean.

questions.stem: Quarterly sales over two years were Year 1: 40, 60, 80, 20 and Year 2: 54, 66, 96, 24. Using the average percentage method, the seasonal index for Q1 is:
questions.explanation: Year 1 mean = 50, so Q1 is 40 ÷ 50 = 80%; Year 2 mean = 60, so Q1 is 54 ÷ 60 = 90%. The seasonal index is the average of these percentages, (80 + 90) ÷ 2 = 85%. 80% and 90% use only one year each.

questions.stem: For the same data (Year 1: 40, 60, 80, 20; Year 2: 54, 66, 96, 24), the seasonal index for Q3 is 160%. This means Q3 sales are typically:
options: 60% above the average quarter
160% above the average quarter
1.6 times the previous quarter's
60% of the average quarter
questions.explanation: In both years Q3 was 160% of the yearly mean (80 ÷ 50 and 96 ÷ 60), so Q3 sales are 1.6 times the average quarter, which is 60% above it. A seasonal index compares a season with the average season, not with the previous season.

questions.stem: To deseasonalise a value in a time series, calculate:
options: actual value − seasonal index
seasonal index ÷ actual value
actual value ÷ seasonal index
actual value × seasonal index
questions.explanation: Dividing by the seasonal index removes the seasonal effect, so values from different seasons can be compared fairly. Multiplying by the seasonal index is the reverse step, used to put seasonality back into a forecast.

questions.stem: Sales in the September quarter were $120 000, and the seasonal index for that quarter is 1.6. The deseasonalised sales are:
questions.explanation: Deseasonalised value = 120 000 ÷ 1.6 = $75 000. Multiplying by the index gives $192 000, which adds seasonality instead of removing it.

questions.stem: A business's seasonal index for summer is 1.25. To deseasonalise summer sales, the actual figures must be:
options: increased by 25%
increased by 20%
decreased by 20%
decreased by 25%
questions.explanation: Deseasonalising divides by 1.25, which is the same as multiplying by 1 ÷ 1.25 = 0.8, a decrease of 20%. Decreasing by 25% would multiply by 0.75, which is a common but incorrect assumption.

questions.stem: A café's sales were $380 000 in Q4 (seasonal index 0.95) and $450 000 in Q1 (seasonal index 1.2). After deseasonalising, which is correct?
options: Q4 performed better: $400 000 compared with $375 000
Q1 performed better: $540 000 compared with $361 000
Q1 performed better: $450 000 compared with $380 000
Both performed equally: each is $390 000 deseasonalised
questions.explanation: Deseasonalised Q4 = 380 000 ÷ 0.95 = $400 000 and Q1 = 450 000 ÷ 1.2 = $375 000, so Q4 was stronger once the season is allowed for. Multiplying by the indices gives $361 000 and $540 000, the reverse of deseasonalising.

questions.stem: Deseasonalised data are useful mainly because they:
options: remove every irregular fluctuation from the time series
convert all quarterly data into yearly totals for comparison
show the trend more clearly by removing the seasonal effect
remove the trend so that only the seasonal pattern remains
questions.explanation: Once seasonality is removed, the underlying trend can be seen and modelled with a least-squares line. Deseasonalising does not remove irregular fluctuations, which remain in the data.

questions.stem: When a least-squares line is fitted to model the trend in a time series, the explanatory variable is:
options: the response
the moving mean
time
the seasonal index
questions.explanation: In a time series the variable of interest depends on when it was recorded, so time (often numbered 1, 2, 3, ...) is the explanatory variable. The variable being measured is the response.

questions.stem: Yearly visitor numbers (thousands) to a national park are modelled by visitors = −12.5t + 840, where t = 1 is 2015. The slope tells us that:
options: visitor numbers are decreasing by about 840 000 per year on average
visitor numbers are decreasing by about 12.5 per year on average
visitor numbers were about 12 500 in the first year recorded
visitor numbers are decreasing by about 12 500 per year on average
questions.explanation: The slope is −12.5 thousand per year, a decrease of about 12 500 visitors each year. Reading the units as plain visitors gives 12.5, and 840 relates to the intercept, not the rate of change.

questions.stem: Deseasonalised quarterly sales follow the trend line y = 3.2t + 150, where t = 1 is the first quarter of the data. The seasonal index for the quarter with t = 13 is 0.85. The forecast actual sales for t = 13 are closest to:
questions.explanation: The trend gives the deseasonalised value 3.2 × 13 + 150 = 191.6. Re-seasonalising multiplies by the index: 191.6 × 0.85 ≈ 162.9. Dividing by the index gives about 225.4, which is the deseasonalising step used in the wrong direction.

questions.stem: A trend line fitted to 3 years of monthly data is used to forecast sales 5 years ahead. The main concern with this forecast is that:
options: it is an interpolation inside the data range, so it is always inaccurate
the seasonal indices must be recalculated using the forecast values first
a least-squares line cannot be fitted to time series data that is monthly
it is an extrapolation well beyond the data, so the trend may not continue
questions.explanation: Forecasting far beyond the period of the data is extrapolation, and the trend may change because of new competitors, prices or events. Forecasts close to the data are more reliable than those far into the future.

questions.stem: Before fitting a least-squares trend line to quarterly sales with strong seasonality, the data should usually be:
options: sorted from smallest to largest, so the line has a positive slope throughout
reduced to the largest quarter of each year, so only peak values are used
deseasonalised, so the line models the trend and not the seasonal ups and downs
multiplied by the seasonal indices, so the seasonal pattern is made stronger
questions.explanation: Strong seasonal swings distort a line fitted to the raw data, so the series is deseasonalised first and the line is fitted to the deseasonalised values. Forecasts from the line are then re-seasonalised by multiplying by the index.

questions.stem: Monthly electricity use for a Brisbane household has a seasonal index of 1.30 for January. The deseasonalised trend forecast for next January is 500 kWh. The forecast actual use is:
options: 530 kWh
500 kWh
650 kWh
385 kWh
questions.explanation: To put the seasonal effect back into a forecast, multiply the deseasonalised value by the index: 500 × 1.30 = 650 kWh. Dividing gives about 385 kWh, which removes seasonality a second time.
